ety.text: Inherited from Northern Middle English fede, feide, from Old French faide, feide, fede, from Proto-West Germanic *faihiþu (“hatred, enmity”) (corresponding to foe + -th), from Proto-Indo-European *peyḱ- (“hostile”). Cognate to Old English fǣhþ, fǣhþu, fǣhþo (“hostility, enmity, violence, revenge, vendetta”), German Fehde, and Dutch vete (“feud”) (directly inherited from Proto-West Germanic) alongside Danish fejde (“feud, enmity, hostility, war”) and Swedish fejd (“feud, controversy, quarrel, strife”) (borrowed from Middle Low German).
From Medieval Latin feudum. Doublet of fee, fief, and feoff.

senses.d: A state of long-standing mutual hostility.
ex: You couldn't call it a feud exactly, but there had always been a chill between Phil Mickelson and Tiger Woods.
Wherein my sword had not impressure made / Of our ranke feud: but the iust gods gainsay,

senses.d: A combination of kindred to avenge injuries or affronts, done or offered to any of their blood, on the offender and all his race.

ex: The two men began to feud after one of them got a job promotion and the other thought he was more qualified.

senses.d: An estate granted to a vassal by a feudal lord in exchange for service.

grp.label: A state of long-standing mutual hostility

ety.text: From Old French querele, from Latin querella (“complaint”), from queror (“to lament, to complain”).

it:faida.gl: feud, especially a continuing conflict between families (typical of the Camorra and Mafia)

ety.text: From Medieval Latin faida, borrowed from Proto-West Germanic *faihiþu (“enmity; feud”).
Borrowed from Latin rīvālitātem. Cognate with obsolete English rivality.

chain.g: enemy, foe (someone who is hostile to, feels hatred towards, opposes the interests of, or intends injury to someone else)

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish enemiztat, enemiztad, evolution of Vulgar Latin *inimīcitātem, from Latin inīmicus, based on inimīcitia. Compare Portuguese inimizade.

pt:rixa.gl: feud (a state of long-standing mutual hostility)

ety.text: From Latin rixa, probably a borrowing.

From Old French fief, borrowed from Medieval Latin fevum, a variant of feudum, from Old Frankish *fehu (“cattle, livestock”), from Proto-Germanic *fehu (“cattle, sheep”), from Proto-Indo-European *peku-, *peḱu- (“sheep”). Cognate with Old High German fihu (“cattle, neat”), Old English feoh (“cattle, property, money”).
